newsitem.title: USA: California researchers link glaucoma to gene.
newsitem.headline: California researchers link glaucoma to gene.

text.p: The most common form of the eye disease glaucoma may be caused by a gene activated by the body's own hormones and by certain molecules, scientists reported on Tuesday.

Researchers at the University of California, San Francisco, said the gene, called TIGR, mass-produces a protein when it is exposed in the eye to the body's steroids and to oxygen-containing molecules called free radicals. Many scientists believe free radicals can damage DNA and the membrane of cells.

The TIGR protein may contribute to the most common form of glaucoma, called primary open-angle glaucoma, the researchers said. Glaucoma affects 3 million to 4 million people in the Unites States and blinds 12,000 of them each year.

The findings were the result of over a decade of research by Jon Polansky, an associate professor of ophthalmology at the University of California, San Francisco, and Thai Nguyen, a molecular biologist there.
The researchers isolated and cloned the gene that encodes the TIGR protein and identified and mapped out the part of the gene that governs how much TIGR protein is produced.
Researchers said the protein produced by the activated TIGR gene causes eye pressure to build up. This pressure is the main cause of optic nerve damage in glaucoma cases.
The researchers found abundant quantities of the TIGR protein in the eyes of patients with primary open-angle glaucoma. Examinations of disease-free eyes revealed much less TIGR.

Polansky said the findings "will give us a way to understand the disease and to block the cause as opposed to treating the symptoms." He said he was developing new drug therapies to suppress the TIGR gene and prevent glaucoma.

The findings were presented at the annual meeting of the Association for Vision in Research and Ophthalmology in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. The results also will appear in the May issue of the journal Ophthalmologica.

The University of California said it had filed patent applications relating to the TIGR gene and had exclusively licensed patent rights for the development of products to InSite Vision Inc of Alameda, California. Polansky was a founder of the company, serves as a consultant and tests some of its drugs.
